title: Sysco Halts All Mexican Lettuce Purchases as Cyclosporiasis Outbreak Kills Two
excerpt: America's largest food distributor stops buying iceberg lettuce from Mexico entirely as the record-breaking parasitic outbreak surpasses 10,000 cases in Michigan alone.
body:
• Sysco, the largest U.S. food distributor, has completely stopped buying iceberg lettuce from Mexico due to the ongoing cyclosporiasis outbreak.
  • Two people have died in Michigan, where over 11,000 cases have been reported — the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak in U.S. history.
  • The FDA has linked the outbreak to iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms' operations in central Mexico, served at Taco Bell restaurants across multiple states.
  • The CDC has recorded over 10,400 lab-confirmed cases nationwide, with more than 12,000 suspected cases still under investigation.

Sysco, the largest food distributor in the United States, has stopped purchasing all iceberg lettuce from Mexico as the country grapples with the worst cyclosporiasis outbreak on record, CEO Kevin Hourican said on Tuesday.

"We're not buying iceberg lettuce from them, and we're not buying it from Mexico. To the degree that we can further diversify our procurement, that is something we're actively working on."

— Kevin Hourican, CEO, Sysco

The decision marks a significant escalation from Sysco's earlier move in mid-July, when it halted sales of Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce specifically. Now the company has cut off all Mexican-sourced iceberg lettuce entirely, shifting procurement to U.S.-grown alternatives.

A Record-Breaking Outbreak

The outbreak, which began in May, has ballooned into the largest cyclosporiasis event ever recorded in the United States. Michigan has been the epicenter, reporting over 11,200 cases statewide, according to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services. Two people in the state have died — both had significant underlying health conditions that officials said may have been worsened by the parasitic infection and associated dehydration.

Nationally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recorded 10,468 laboratory-confirmed cases across multiple states, along with more than 12,255 suspected cases awaiting confirmation. Data from healthcare analytics firm Truveta showed cyclosporiasis diagnoses in July were more than 11 times the eight-year average for that month.

The Taylor Farms Connection

An FDA investigation has linked the outbreak to iceberg lettuce sourced from Taylor Farms de Mexico, a privately held supplier based in Guanajuato, central Mexico. The contaminated lettuce was produced as 5-pound bags and widely distributed to hospitals, ballparks, and fast-food chains, according to Reuters.

Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled certain iceberg lettuce products sold under the Taylor Fresh Foods and Marketside brands, though the company has maintained that the FDA has not identified a confirmed positive test result for Cyclospora — describing an earlier positive border sample as a false positive.

The FDA, however, has said its basis for linking Taylor Farms' Mexico lettuce to the outbreak remains unchanged, citing traceback and epidemiological evidence.

The outbreak was first identified through cases at Taco Bell restaurants in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and West Virginia, where shredded iceberg lettuce was served. The investigation has since expanded to nine states.

Supply Chain Ripple Effects

Sysco's decision to cut off Mexican lettuce underscores the broader supply chain disruption caused by the outbreak. The company acknowledged that replacing Taylor Farms' volume — the largest lettuce producer in the U.S. — poses a logistical challenge.

"It's a high quality, high integrity shop, but we've had to take actions. We've moved source of product away from them to the degree that we can. Because they're really big, you can't just turn it off overnight."

— Kevin Hourican, CEO, Sysco

Reduced consumer demand for lettuce, driven by food safety concerns, has paradoxically made it easier for Sysco to source domestically. Former FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb noted last week that some large retailers and restaurants were shunning produce from other growers in central Mexico out of fear about broader contamination.

What You Need to Know

Cyclosporiasis is caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis, typically contracted through food or water contaminated with human feces. Symptoms include severe watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, bloating, nausea, and fatigue. If untreated, the illness can persist for weeks or even months.

While generally not life-threatening, the CDC has noted that children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems face higher risks. The two Michigan deaths — the first fatalities linked to the outbreak — have heightened public alarm.

Health officials emphasize that thoroughly washing produce does not reliably eliminate Cyclospora, making source-level controls critical. Consumers concerned about food safety are advised to stay updated through the CDC and FDA outbreak tracking pages and to seek medical attention if symptoms develop after eating raw salads or greens.

What Comes Next

Federal investigators continue tracing the outbreak's full scope, and the FDA has not ruled out additional contamination sources beyond Taylor Farms. Cuts to federal health agencies have complicated the response, according to former CDC officials and food safety experts.

Sysco reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday despite the outbreak, with sales rising 4.7% to $22.12 billion and adjusted earnings of $1.53 per share beating analyst expectations. The company forecast fiscal year 2027 sales growth of 6% to 7%.
